author: MrinankSharma
text: In short, modelling must reflect time-varying uncertainty in the effectiveness of NPIs; real-time monitoring of NPI effects, transmission, and the rise of novel variants is vital to allow continued, safe reopening of society. 13/

author: MrinankSharma
text: Still today, more people avoid crowded spaces than in March 2020, and organisational safety measures remain in place. But we cannot expect our estimates to generalise perfectly to today, given vaccine-induced behaviour changes and the rise of new variants. 12/

author: MrinankSharma
text: We find that second-wave estimates outperform previous, first-wave, estimates at predicting transmission in Europe’s third wave (January to May 2020). In the third wave, behaviour and safety measures remained relatively stable and similar to the second wave. 11/

author: MrinankSharma
text: The situation today is different to resurgence. Delta emerged, causing fourth and fifth waves despite widespread vaccination coverage in several countries. Intervention effects continue to evolve, calling for real-time monitoring and flexible policy.  10/

author: MrinankSharma
text: Further, strict mask-wearing mandates were associated with moderate decreases in transmission in our analysis. Governments may be able to curtail transmission, if necessary, by reintroducing mask-wearing, a policy that still allows society to reopen. 9/

author: MrinankSharma
text: Our results suggest that safer operation of educational institutions, including schools and universities, is possible with stringent organisational safety measures. This is reason for optimism, if similar measures are taken in the future.  8/

author: MrinankSharma
text: A striking difference is in closing educational institutions, which was associated with large decreases in transmission in March 2020, but much smaller decreases in the resurgence. 7/

author: MrinankSharma
text: Interventions had smaller effects in the 2nd wave. The most stringent interventions per region reduced R by 50%, compared to 80% in the first wave. The difference may be due to organisational safety measures and personal protective behaviours enabling safer public life. 6/

author: MrinankSharma
text: We give the first effectiveness estimates for different interventions in Europe’s resurgence of COVID-19, between August 2020 and January 2021. This uncovers large differences in the effects of NPIs between pandemic waves. 5/ https://t.co/gexFWK06df

author: MrinankSharma
text: We collect the largest dataset of NPI implementation dates across Europe, spanning 114 European Regions across 7 countries. The dataset has over 5500 NPI entries with semi-independent double entry to ensure high data quality. 4/

author: MrinankSharma
text: For example, we can’t assume that closing schools in March 2020 is the same as closing schools in early 2021 or today. What it *means* for schools to be open is different. Reduced class sizes, outdoor activities, and more affect transmission in schools. 3/

author: MrinankSharma
text: Understanding how government measures affect transmission is crucial for policy decisions—which NPIs can we lift while protecting healthcare? Most previous estimates are from the first wave (March 2020), but they don’t reflect how society restructured to make life safer!  2/

author: MrinankSharma

author: MrinankSharma
text: Finally, we mathematically ground the interpretation of NPI effectiveness estimates when certain common assumptions do not hold.  7/8

author: MrinankSharma
text: Models which account for noise in disease transmission compare favourably. Focusing on these models, we find that previously published results are robust across these choices and across different models. 6/8 https://t.co/mIIiNeSq8r

author: MrinankSharma
text: We investigate 2 prior models and propose 6 variants with different *structural assumptions*. We assess how well these models generalise to unseen countries and how sensitive their estimates are to unobserved factors e.g., unrecorded NPIs. 5/8 https://t.co/3jVh9DsOBM

author: MrinankSharma
text: But these models make assumptions! Assumed parameter values … limited datasets … model structure. If the results are highly sensitive to these assumptions, how can they be used to guide policy? 4/8

author: MrinankSharma
text: Data-driven NPI models link the NPIs (government interventions) that each country implemented to observed cases and deaths. We can perform Bayesian inference to estimate the effectiveness of each NPI. 3/8

author: MrinankSharma
text: Inferring how effective government interventions (NPIs) were at controlling COVID-19 would help control the epidemic while also minimizing the burden placed on the population. 2/8
